items.prompt: In a perspective drawing, what does the horizon line represent?

options.label: The edge of the paper's frame
The lightest area of the scene
The viewer's eye level
The ground under the nearest object

rubric: The horizon line marks the viewer's eye level.
Distractors confuse it with the ground, value or the page edge.

items.prompt: In drawing, what does the term 'value' refer to?

options.label: How expensive the materials are
How light or dark an area is
How thick a line is
How sharp the pencil point is

rubric: Value is the lightness or darkness of an area.
Distractors mix value up with line weight or materials.

items.prompt: What is a vanishing point?

options.label: The darkest spot in a shaded area, where light is blocked
The point where the horizon line meets the edge of the paper
Where parallel receding lines appear to meet
The centre point of the paper, where all lines must cross

rubric: Parallel lines receding from the viewer appear to converge at a vanishing point.
Distractors confuse it with shading or the page centre.

items.prompt: Which of these graphite pencils makes the softest, darkest mark?

options.label: HB
2H
4H
6B

rubric: B grades are soft and dark, and a higher number means softer.
H grades are hard and light; HB sits in the middle.

items.prompt: What is the name for a quick drawing that captures the movement and pose of a figure?

options.label: Cross-hatching
Stippling
Gesture drawing
Blind contour

rubric: Gesture drawing captures movement and pose quickly.
The other terms are a contour method and shading techniques.

items.prompt: Which of the following are techniques for building up value (shading) with a pencil? Select all that apply.

options.label: Vanishing point
Stippling
Horizon line
Hatching
Cross-hatching

rubric: Hatching, cross-hatching and stippling build value with marks.
Horizon line and vanishing point belong to perspective, not shading.

items.prompt: A learner wants to draw a simple box in one-point perspective. They have a ruler and a blank page. According to the standard method, which step should they do first?

options.label: Draw the front face of the box as a square, then add depth
Shade the darkest side of the box to set the light direction
Draw a horizon line and mark one vanishing point on it
Sketch the cast shadow so the box sits firmly on the ground

rubric: One-point perspective starts with the horizon line and a vanishing point.
Distractors are later steps: shading, shadow and texture.

items.prompt: Why do many drawing teachers ask beginners to break a subject into basic shapes first?

options.label: It lets beginners finish a drawing faster by skipping fine detail
It removes the need to keep looking at the subject while drawing
It sets the proportions and structure before any details
It makes the lines darker and more confident from the start

rubric: Basic shapes establish structure and proportion first.
Distractors claim speed or skipping observation, which is not the purpose.

items.prompt: Why does overlapping one object in front of another help suggest depth in a drawing?

options.label: Overlapping objects are drawn at the same size, which shows they sit side by side
The overlapped edge is drawn with a lighter line, so it looks farther away
The front object hides part of the one behind, so it reads as closer
Both objects are placed on the horizon line, which makes them look stacked

rubric: Partial hiding signals that one object is nearer.
Distractors invent rules about size, line weight or the horizon.

items.prompt: A ball sits on a table with the light source high on the upper left. Where will its cast shadow fall?

options.label: On the top of the ball, facing the light
To the lower right, on the table
Directly behind the ball, on the far wall
To the upper left, toward the light

rubric: Shadows fall away from the light, so lower right here.
Distractors put the shadow toward the light or on the lit side.

items.prompt: Why is drawing from observation said to work better than drawing from memory for a beginner?

options.label: Observation lets you skip the early sketching stage entirely
Memory images are always far too detailed to put on paper
Pencil marks come out darker and more confident when you look
Looking makes you draw the shapes you see, not stored symbols

rubric: Observing real shapes replaces stored symbols like a stick-figure eye.
Distractors give false claims about detail, skipped steps or darkness.

items.prompt: A drawing has outlines of identical thickness everywhere and looks flat. How would varying line weight help?

options.label: Thicker lines everywhere would replace shading for form
Thinner lines on all edges would raise the horizon line
Heavier lines on shadowed or nearer edges add depth
Thicker lines on distant edges would make them look closer

rubric: Heavier lines on nearer or shadowed edges suggest depth and emphasis.
Distractors give effects that line weight does not produce.

items.prompt: Which of these help a shaded sphere look round rather than flat? Select all that apply.

options.label: Filling it with one even grey tone
A cast shadow that grounds it on the surface
A core shadow on the side away from the light
A gradual change from light to dark across the surface
A heavy outline of equal weight and no shading

rubric: Gradual value shifts, a core shadow and a cast shadow show form.
Uniform outlines or even tones give no sense of volume.

items.prompt: A beginner draws a mug seen from slightly above. They draw the rim as a shape with pointed ends, like a lemon, and it looks wrong. What is the best explanation?

options.label: The rim is a circle, so it should be drawn as a perfect circle even from above
Pointed ends are right for a tilted rim, but the lines are too light to read
The mug needs a vanishing point at each end of the rim to fix the corners
A tilted circle becomes an ellipse with rounded ends, not points

rubric: A circle viewed at an angle becomes an ellipse with rounded ends.
Distractors suggest a flat circle, line darkness or extra vanishing points.

items.prompt: Why do many artists begin a drawing with light construction lines before adding final contours?

options.label: They give the paper a toned surface that makes shading easier later
They let you check proportion and placement before committing to dark lines
They remove the need to look at the subject while drawing the details
They make the final outline thicker and more confident automatically

rubric: Light construction lines are easy to adjust, so errors in proportion and placement are caught early.
Distractors treat the lines as a line-weight or toning trick rather than a planning step.

items.prompt: A sphere is lit from the upper left. Where does the core shadow, the darkest part of the form, sit?

options.label: Along the very outer edge of the sphere on the lit side
On the lower right, away from the light, inside the edge
On the upper left, where the light hits the form most directly
In a flat even band running across the centre of the sphere

rubric: The core shadow lies on the side turned away from the light, just inside the edge where bounced light lightens the rim.
Distractors confuse the light side with the dark side or assume shading is uniform.

items.prompt: You draw a street scene from a crouching position instead of standing. What happens to the horizon line in your drawing?

options.label: It sits lower on the page, because it matches your lower eye level
It disappears, because the ground blocks the view of the horizon
It stays in the same place, because the horizon is fixed on the scene
It moves higher on the page, because you are closer to the ground

rubric: The horizon line is the viewer's eye level, so a lower viewpoint lowers it.
Distractors treat the horizon as fixed or reverse the relationship.

items.prompt: In a drawing, a pear is partly covered by an apple. What does this overlap tell the viewer?

options.label: The apple is larger in real life than the pear is
The pear is closer, since it is drawn more completely
Both are the same distance away, sharing the same space
The apple is closer to the viewer than the pear

rubric: An object that covers part of another reads as nearer.
Distractors misread overlap as showing completeness, equal depth or real size.

items.prompt: Why does drawing the negative space around a chair often improve accuracy?

options.label: It lets you skip measuring the chair's real proportions
It makes the chair darker so that its edges are stronger
It makes you see plain shapes rather than your idea of a chair
It means the chair needs no overlapping or perspective cues

rubric: Negative space shapes have no symbolic meaning, so you draw what you see instead of what you assume.
Distractors claim it replaces measuring or changes tone or perspective.

items.prompt: Which of these are cues that make objects look farther away in a flat drawing? Select all that apply.

options.label: Distant objects drawn larger and with darker, sharper edges
Lines that converge toward a vanishing point
Overlapping, where nearer shapes cover farther ones
Lower contrast and softer detail in distant objects

rubric: Overlap, convergence and atmospheric softening all suggest depth.
Drawing distant objects larger and sharper reverses the depth cues.

items.prompt: A learner draws a coffee mug from slightly above. The rim is an ellipse, but she draws it with pointed ends like a lemon. The mug looks like a flat cut-out. What does this error show she misunderstands?

options.label: A rim seen from slightly above should flatten into a straight line
A tilted circle becomes an ellipse with smoothly rounded ends
The far edge of the rim should be drawn narrower than the near edge
A mug's rim has corners where it meets the handle, so its ends should be sharp

rubric: The rim is a circle in perspective, which becomes an ellipse with rounded ends; pointed ends break the curve.
Distractors invent corners or incorrect rules about the rim's shape.

items.prompt: At arm's length, a bottle measures 6 units tall and 2 units wide against your pencil. You draw the bottle 12 cm tall. How wide should you draw it?

options.label: 4 cm
3 cm
2 cm
6 cm

rubric: The ratio 6:2 is 3:1, so 12 cm tall means 4 cm wide.
Distractors come from not scaling or from the wrong ratio.

items.prompt: You draw a box in one-point perspective with its front face toward you. Which edge of the front face stays exactly horizontal?

options.label: The top edge of the front face
None, since all edges must tilt toward the vanishing point
Only the bottom edge, since it is closest to the ground
The edge running from the front corner to the vanishing point

rubric: In one-point perspective, the face parallel to the picture plane keeps true horizontals and verticals.
Distractors apply convergence to the front face or favour one edge.

items.prompt: A hatched area of your drawing looks too light, but you want to keep the pencil marks visible. What is the best next step?

options.label: Press harder to flatten the first layer into one solid tone
Erase the lines and draw a single thick outline around it
Add a second layer of hatching crossing the first at an angle
Smudge the whole area with a finger until the lines vanish

rubric: Cross-hatching deepens value while keeping a visible, controlled mark structure.
Distractors lose the marks or swap shading for outline.

items.prompt: You are drawing a standing adult using the rule of about 7.5 heads tall. The head is 4 cm tall on your page. About how tall should the whole figure be?

options.label: 28 cm
16 cm
40 cm
30 cm

rubric: 4 cm multiplied by 7.5 is 30 cm.
Distractors come from using the wrong head count or a wrong multiplication.

items.prompt: A ball sits on a table with the light coming from the left. Where do you draw its cast shadow?

options.label: On the ball's lit side, as a darker patch next to the highlight
On the table to the left of the ball, stretching toward the light source
Directly under the ball only, with no extension to either side
On the table to the right of the ball, darkest at the contact point

rubric: Cast shadows fall away from the light and are darkest at the contact point.
Distractors put the shadow on the light side or confuse cast shadow with form shadow.

items.prompt: You are drawing a cube in two-point perspective. Which steps are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Draw a horizon line and place two vanishing points on it
Aim the receding edges toward the two vanishing points
Tilt the vertical edges slightly so they also converge toward a third point below the cube
Keep the vertical edges of the cube vertical

rubric: Two-point perspective uses two vanishing points on the horizon, vertical edges stay vertical, and receding edges converge.
Parallel receding edges would remove the perspective effect.

items.prompt: You are drawing an apple lit from the right. Your first pass shades the left half in one even grey, and the apple looks flat like a disc. Which change best fixes it?

options.label: Darken the whole shaded half evenly, so the contrast with the lit side grows
Grade the shading, darkest at the core shadow, with a lighter reflected edge
Remove all shading and rely on colour to show the roundness
Outline the apple with a thicker line so that its edge stands out

rubric: A gradual shift in value, with a core shadow and reflected light, describes a rounded form.
Distractors keep the form flat by using uniform tone, outline or no shading.

items.prompt: You are drawing a cube in two-point perspective. The horizon line and both vanishing points are set, and you have drawn the vertical edge nearest the viewer. What is the next step?

options.label: Draw horizontal lines across from the top and bottom of the front edge
Draw lines from the top and bottom of that edge to each vanishing point
Draw the far edges first, then fit the front edge between them
Draw the back vertical edge at the same height as the front edge

rubric: Receding edges of the two visible faces must run to the vanishing points from the ends of the nearest edge.
Horizontal lines and equal-height back edges are one-point or flat-view habits that break two-point perspective.

items.prompt: At arm's length, a vase measures 4 cm tall and 3 cm wide along your pencil. You draw the vase 12 cm tall. How wide should you draw it to keep the same proportion?

options.label: 16 cm
12 cm
8 cm
9 cm

rubric: The scale factor is 3 (12 / 4), so the width becomes 3 x 3 = 9 cm.
Adding the same amount to both measures, instead of scaling both, gives wrong widths like 11 or 8 cm.

items.prompt: A single light source sits high and to the upper left of a sphere resting on a flat table. Where do you draw the cast shadow?

options.label: On the sphere itself, as a band along its upper left edge facing the light
On the table to the upper left, beneath the light and set apart from the sphere
On the table directly beneath the sphere, as a small circle hidden behind it
On the table to the lower right, touching the sphere's base

rubric: Cast shadows fall on the opposite side of the object from the light and connect at the contact point.
Placing the shadow on the light side confuses cast shadow with highlight or form shadow.

items.prompt: You are drawing a street scene with the horizon line at your own standing eye level. Two adults of equal height stand on level ground, one close and one far away. Where do you place the heads?

options.label: The near figure's head sits on the horizon, and the far one is drawn lower
The far figure's head sits above the horizon, as it is farther away
Both heads touch the horizon line, with the far figure drawn smaller
Both heads sit at the same height on the page, with equal sizes

rubric: Where the viewer's eye level matches head height, every same-height standing head lies on the horizon line, with size shrinking with distance.
Distractors ignore that the horizon marks eye level or treat distance as vertical offset.

items.prompt: You want a smooth, gradual tone running from light paper to a deep shadow on a drawn cloth fold using hatching. Which procedure fits best?

options.label: Use one layer of lines with firm pressure, changing line direction sharply wherever the tone steps darker
Build several light hatched layers, adding more layers and closer lines toward the dark end
Draw the dark end first with heavy pressure, then erase gradually toward the light end to blend it
Press hard with one pass of widely spaced lines at the dark end, leaving the rest bare paper

rubric: Layering with controlled spacing and pressure produces smooth, adjustable gradation.
One-pass hard lines and abrupt changes give streaky, stepped tone.

items.prompt: You are starting a drawing of a chair from observation. Which steps fit a sound block-in stage? Select all that apply.

options.label: Check key angles against an imagined vertical or horizontal
Compare the negative spaces between the legs to verify shapes
Finish the texture of the seat before placing other parts
Establish the overall height-to-width proportion with a few large shapes
Outline the whole chair in dark, final lines first

rubric: Block-in relies on big proportions, angle checks and negative-space comparison before detail.
Finishing one area early or committing to dark lines locks in errors.

items.prompt: You are drawing a long fence receding along a straight road toward a vanishing point on the horizon. The nearest post is drawn 10 cm tall, and the posts are equally spaced in reality. You have placed the nearest post and the vanishing point. What do you do next to place the other posts convincingly?

options.label: Space the posts equally on the page, and curve the line through their tops toward the horizon
Draw every post at the same height, and raise each one on the page to suggest distance
Run lines from the post's top and base to the vanishing point, and shrink the spacing
Make each following post 1 cm shorter than the last, and space them equally on the page

rubric: Post tops and bases lie on lines converging to the vanishing point, and spacing foreshortens progressively with distance.
Equal spacing or equal heights ignore perspective foreshortening.

items.prompt: A student's drawing of a cup looks as if it is tilting forward. The cup's base ellipse has sharp, pointed ends and a flat bottom edge. What is the most likely cause of the problem?

options.label: The ellipse is too wide, where it should match the cup's height
The ellipse ends are pointed, where they should be smoothly rounded curves
The ellipse is drawn with one stroke, where it should be drawn in segments
The base ellipse is too dark, where it should be lighter than the rim

rubric: Ellipses in perspective have rounded ends, and pointed or flat shapes read as distorted form.
Width, darkness and stroke count are not the fault shown in the description.

items.prompt: In a frontal portrait the face looks wrong, as if the features were pasted high on the head. The eyes sit close to the top of the skull outline. What construction error best explains this?

options.label: The eyes sit above the head's midpoint, leaving too little skull above
The chin was drawn too narrow and short, which compresses the lower half of the face and pushes the mouth and nose upward
The ears were aligned with the brow and nose instead of set lower, which pulls the whole feature set up toward the crown
The nose was placed too close to the mouth, so the lower face looks short and the features seem to crowd upward

rubric: The eyes sit roughly halfway down the head, and placing them near the top leaves features crowded high.
Ear, nose and chin faults produce different distortions.

items.prompt: A shaded sphere reads as a flat disc. The tone runs smoothly from light at the center to the darkest value at the outline, with no lighter band along the edge. What explains the flatness?

options.label: The darkest tone sits at the edge with no reflected light, so there is no core shadow
The cast shadow beneath the sphere is missing, so the form has nothing to anchor its roundness to the ground
The gradient is too smooth and even, so the form needs hard-edged value steps to show its planes turning
The highlight is too small and sharp, so it should be enlarged to cover much of the lit side of the sphere

rubric: Darkest tone at the edge with no reflected light makes a radial disc, not a sphere with a core shadow and reflected light.
Smooth gradients are fine, and a cast shadow alone does not fix form shading.

items.prompt: Two drawings of the same box use the same outline. One uses uniform line weight, and the other uses heavier lines on bottom edges and the near corner and lighter lines on far edges. Why does the second look deeper?

options.label: Lighter lines remove far edges, so the shape looks simpler in space
Heavier lines make the box look physically larger than the first
Line weight variation signals nearness and weight, which suggests overlap and depth
Uniform lines look mechanical, which makes the first box look flatter on paper

rubric: Heavier lines on near and shaded edges and lighter lines on far edges create cues for depth and weight.
Size, simplification and mechanical look are not the depth mechanism.

items.prompt: A student draws a forearm pointing straight toward the viewer, side by side with the hand, and it looks like a stump. What is the root cause?

options.label: The student outlined the arm with heavy contour lines, which flattens it and removes the sense of depth
The student shaded the arm with even tone, which flattened the muscle shapes and hid the arm's form
The student drew the hand too small, so the arm looks oversized and stubby beside it, and enlarging the hand would fix it
The student did not foreshorten the arm, drawing its true length instead of its compressed, overlapping look

rubric: Forms pointing toward the viewer look compressed, with overlaps, so drawing true length breaks the illusion.
Hand size, contour and even shading do not explain the stump look.

items.prompt: A still life of fruit and a jug looks flat even though the proportions are accurate. Which are likely contributing causes? Select all that apply.

options.label: No objects overlap, so depth order is hard to read
The objects are placed near the middle of the page
The pencil is slightly too soft for the paper's grain
Every edge has the same sharpness, near or far
All objects have almost the same value range and contrast

rubric: Depth reads through value contrast, overlap and edge variation, and their absence flattens a drawing.
Pencil softness and central placement do not directly flatten depth.

items.prompt: A learner copies photos accurately using a grid, but their drawings from life, such as a mug on a desk, keep coming out with distorted proportions. They use the same pencil and paper, and they do not measure or compare angles from life. Which explanation best accounts for the difference?

options.label: A photo is already flat, so the grid skips the 3D-to-2D translation that life drawing needs
Life drawing needs thicker, bolder lines to show the mug's edges, and thin lines distort its proportions
The photo has more even lighting than a desk scene, so its values read more clearly and are easier to copy
The grid trains the hand to control line, but that control does not carry over to drawing from life

rubric: Copying a photo avoids the 3D-to-2D translation, which life drawing requires through measurement and comparison.
Lighting, line control and thickness do not explain why the proportions fail.

items.prompt: A student draws a white cup on white cloth with an accurate outline, yet it looks flat. Her values all sit in a narrow mid-grey range. What is the most likely cause of the flatness?

options.label: White objects cannot be drawn in graphite without a toned ground, so the form cannot be shown
The outline is too even in weight, which by itself removes any sense of volume from a rounded object
The rim ellipse is slightly too narrow, and that single error flattens the entire body of the cup
No clear step between lit plane, core shadow and cast shadow, so the form's turning is never stated

rubric: Compressed values with no distinct light, core shadow and cast shadow steps hide how the surface turns.
Distractors blame outline weight, a minor ellipse error or the medium, none of which explains the narrow value range.

items.prompt: In a two-point perspective drawing of a building, the near corner looks stretched and distorted. The vanishing points were placed 12 cm apart on the horizon line. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Vanishing points too close together force steep convergence, like an extreme wide-angle view
Vertical edges were kept parallel to the page, when they should converge toward a third point to look believable
The two sets of receding lines were not drawn at equal angles, so the corner cannot close properly
The horizon line sits too low, which stretches the nearest vertical edge of the box toward the viewer

rubric: Close vanishing points create exaggerated convergence and distortion near the corner.
Distractors misstate horizon effects, wrongly require converging verticals, or assume equal angles are needed.

items.prompt: A student draws a seated model whose thigh points toward the viewer. She draws the thigh at its full length, and the figure looks broken at the hip. What went wrong?

options.label: She overlapped the thigh with the lower leg, which never occurs in foreshortened poses of the body
She shaded the thigh too dark, and tone alone is enough to shorten a limb in a drawing
She used a head-count canon, which cannot be applied to seated figures at any viewing angle
She drew the thigh from knowledge of its real length instead of measuring its compressed visible length

rubric: Foreshortening requires drawing what is seen, measured against other parts, rather than what is known.
Distractors invoke overlap rules, canon limits or tone, none of which cause the broken hip.

items.prompt: A pencil portrait has accurate shapes, yet looks like a cutout pasted on the page. Every edge of the head is drawn with the same crisp, dark line. What is missing?

options.label: Sharper detail in the background, so the head looks set within a believable space that surrounds it
Heavier hatching inside the head, since interior tone is what separates a rounded figure from the flat paper
A thicker outline overall, which pushes the head forward from the background and gives the shape more weight
Variation between hard and soft edges, so turning or background-matching edges dissolve

rubric: Lost-and-found edges integrate the form with its surroundings; uniform hard edges create a cutout look.
Distractors add weight, tone or background detail, which do not address uniform edge quality.

items.prompt: Drawing a barn from life, a learner's roofline always ends up steeper than the real one, though his proportions are otherwise sound. Which habit most likely explains it?

options.label: Judging the slope by eye against an imagined angle rather than checking it against a true horizontal or vertical
Holding the pencil out at arm's length to measure the slope, with the elbow bent a little so the angle reads steeper
Drawing with a soft pencil, whose broader line tends to exaggerate the steepness of the larger angles in a sketch
Starting with the roof before the walls, so that early angles set the tilt that later angles are measured against

rubric: Angles are reliably judged only against a true horizontal or vertical reference, not by memory or impression.
Distractors blame drawing order, pencil softness or measuring posture, none of which systematically steepen angles.

items.prompt: A sphere drawn with a smooth gradient from white to black across its face still looks like a flat disc. Which causes help explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Darkest value placed at the very edge, ignoring reflected light returning into the shadow side
Use of graphite, which cannot show roundness without coloured pigment
No distinct core shadow band separating the lit side from the shadow side
A perfectly circular outline, which always reads as two-dimensional regardless of tone
No cast shadow tying the sphere to a surface beneath it

rubric: Core shadow, cast shadow and reflected light are the cues that turn a gradient into a rounded, grounded form.
Distractors blame the circular outline or the medium, neither of which prevents roundness.

items.prompt: A learner draws a portrait from a model. Every feature is accurate in shape, but the face reads as a child's. The eyes sit about 60% of the way down from crown to chin, and the model is an adult. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The jaw was drawn too narrow, which pulls the eyes down relative to the chin and makes the lower face look small
The cranium was overestimated, so the eyes sit below the head's midline, where a child's do
The nose was drawn too short, which shifts the eye line down because the nose sets the face's vertical scale
The eyes were drawn too large, which makes the whole face read younger even when positions are correct

rubric: Adult eyes sit near the head's midline; placing them lower from an oversized cranium gives a childlike look.
Distractors blame single features instead of the underlying placement error.

items.prompt: Halfway through a drawing, a learner suspects a proportion error but cannot see it after an hour of looking. Which check best meets the criterion of exposing errors the eye has adapted to?

options.label: Darken the questionable contours so the structure stands out and can be judged as it is
Erase the whole drawing and restart from memory, so the earlier bias cannot recur
View the drawing and subject in a mirror or flipped, so familiar shapes read as new
Stare longer at the problem area while adding finer detail, so the mismatch becomes obvious

rubric: Mirroring or flipping breaks adaptation and reveals proportion errors quickly.
Distractors extend the same viewing, reinforce the lines, or discard work while keeping the same bias.

items.prompt: A student draws a bright white egg on dark cloth. Criterion: the egg must read as the lightest object, and paper white is the lightest value available. Which approach best meets it?

options.label: Leave the egg's lit side as bare paper and darken the cloth beside it, so contrast does the work
Outline the egg in a heavy dark line, which makes it read as brightest by contrast with the cloth
Darken the egg's shadow side as far as the pencil allows, leaving the cloth pale so it glows
Tone the egg's lit side lightly so it can be lifted later, keeping the cloth at an even mid value

rubric: Brightness is relative; preserving paper white and darkening the surround maximises the contrast available.
Distractors spend the lightest value early, rely on outline, or lighten the background and lose the contrast.

items.prompt: A landscape study shows distant hills drawn with the same dark, sharp contrast as the foreground trees. Criterion: convincing depth with minimal changes. Which critique and fix is strongest?

options.label: Reduce the size of the hills; scale alone creates depth, so values and edges can stay unchanged
Outline the hills more heavily and add texture, so they hold their position behind the trees
Lighten and soften the hills, reserving the darkest darks and sharpest edges for the foreground to suggest air
Add a ruled horizon and converging lines, since linear perspective is the only reliable depth cue here

rubric: Atmospheric perspective reduces contrast and edge sharpness with distance and is the quickest fix.
Distractors strengthen the hills, rely on scale alone, or insist linear perspective is the only cue.

items.prompt: A learner's drawing of a room with a bed, a table and a window has several flaws. Judged by the criterion 'the viewer must believe the objects share one space,' which flaw is most damaging?

options.label: The table's cast shadow is a little too soft near its legs on the floor
Each object has its own horizon line, so no two objects share an eye level
The window frame's lines are slightly wobbly rather than ruled with a straightedge
Line weight is uniform across foreground and background objects throughout the whole drawing

rubric: Inconsistent eye level breaks the single viewpoint and the sense of shared space.
The other flaws are real but secondary to shared-space believability.

items.prompt: For a 10-minute figure study, the criteria are speed, easy correction, and keeping the paper's lights intact. Which shading method best fits?

options.label: Fine cross-hatching on the face with careful detail, then leaving the body unshaded for time
Heavy blended graphite smudged with a finger over the whole figure, then lifted back to find the lights
Light directional hatching built up from lights to darks along the form, leaving paper bare in the highlights
A hard dark contour, then pressing dark fill into every shadow shape at full strength from the start

rubric: Light hatching built gradually is fast, correctable and preserves the lights.
Distractors dull the lights, commit to darks too early, or use time on detail unevenly.

items.prompt: A learner uses photo references to practise seeing accurately. Which statements are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Wide-angle lenses distort near edges, so perspective cues may need checking against the horizon
Photos give the same depth information as life, so copying them builds identical observational skill
Gridding a photo trains the same proportion judgement as measuring from a live subject
Photos compress shadows and highlights, so values may need reinterpreting rather than copying directly

rubric: Photos compress value range and can distort perspective, so they need critical reading.
Distractors claim photos equal life or that gridding builds the same judgement as measuring.

items.prompt: A learner has 40 minutes to draw a seated model lit from one side, aiming for a convincing pose, proportion and light. She is deciding how to spend the time. Which plan best meets those criteria?

options.label: Render the head fully first as the focal point, then fit the body to it using the remaining time
Start with gesture and overall proportions, then mass in light and shadow shapes, saving detail for last
Begin by shading the shadow side of the whole body, then add contours once the form emerges
Draw a complete clean outline of the whole figure, then shade each area from left to right

rubric: Working from whole to part secures pose, proportion and lighting before time runs out.
Distractors finish one area early, commit to outlines before relationships are checked, or skip structure.

items.prompt: A tonal drawing of a still life has accurate shapes, but it looks flat because every edge is equally sharp and dark. Judged by the criterion of convincing depth, which revision is best?

options.label: Raise the contrast across the whole sheet so the darkest darks and lightest lights appear in every area of the drawing
Vary edge quality, crisp at the focal point and softer or lost elsewhere
Add hatching texture to the surfaces so that the materials are identified and each object reads as distinct
Darken the outlines of the forms nearest the viewer so that each one separates clearly from its neighbours

rubric: Varying edge sharpness (lost and found edges) creates atmosphere and a focal hierarchy.
Uniform lines, texture or contrast flatten the image because nothing recedes.

items.prompt: You have 20 minutes to draw a standing model from life, and you need to catch proportion errors early. Which approach best meets the criteria of speed and early error detection?

options.label: Block in large shapes with angles and plumb-line checks, then correct before adding detail
Trace each contour from top to bottom, trusting continuous line to hold the proportions
Finish the head first, then measure each other part against it in turn
Lay a grid over the sheet and copy each cell, since a grid guarantees accurate proportion

rubric: Checking big relationships first exposes errors while they are cheap to fix.
Finishing parts sequentially lets early errors accumulate, and a grid is impractical for a live pose.

items.prompt: In a two-point perspective street scene, the artist places both vanishing points only a little way apart, inside the sheet. Which is the most serious consequence for believability?

options.label: All depth cues vanish, because strongly converging lines flatten the picture plane
The horizon line is lost, because vanishing points close together cannot share a horizon
Forms near the sides look badly distorted, because receding edges converge at very steep angles
Line weight becomes uneven, because lines running toward close points grow too long

rubric: Close vanishing points cause wide-angle-style distortion, with sharply skewed corners.
Both points still lie on one horizon, and the convergence exaggerates depth rather than removing it.

items.prompt: For a 15-minute study that must establish broad tonal masses and allow quick restatement of the lights, which medium is the best trade-off?

options.label: A hard 4H pencil, because it gives a precise, clean line that holds exact edges
Vine charcoal, because it covers large areas fast and lifts readily to restate lights
Fine-liner pen, because permanent marks force decisive and accurate commitments
A 2mm mechanical pencil, because it keeps a constant point so values stay consistent

rubric: Vine charcoal suits fast massing and easy lifting and correction.
Hard pencils, pens and fine leads are slow for broad tone and hard to revise.

items.prompt: A student's sphere shows the reflected-light zone at the lower edge rendered lighter than the halftone on the lit side, so the form looks flat and glowing. Evaluating the rendering of form, what is the main flaw?

options.label: Reflected light is too bright; it should stay darker than the halftone, just above the core shadow
The highlight is too small, so the form does not read as shiny; enlarging it would restore the sense of volume
The cast shadow is too dark and competes with the lit side; lightening it would restore the correct value order
The terminator is too crisp, so softening it until it disappears would make the transition read as smooth form

rubric: Reflected light should stay within the shadow family, lighter than the core shadow but darker than the halftone.
Erasing the terminator or enlarging the highlight does not fix the value ordering.

items.prompt: A drawing of a flat plain shows three adult figures of equal height. The nearest has its head on the horizon, but the farthest has its head far above it. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: The farthest figure's feet should be nearer the horizon than the nearest figure's feet
The horizon should be lowered to the feet to repair the inconsistency
The farthest figure should be drawn larger so the depth is emphasised
The farthest head should sit on the horizon, as eye level equals head height on flat ground

rubric: For equal-height figures on flat ground, all heads meet the horizon and feet rise toward it with distance.
Enlarging distant figures or moving the horizon to the feet breaks the perspective logic.

items.prompt: A student draws a white cup beside black cloth under a window. The cup's lit side is bare white paper and the cloth is solid black, so the cup looks pasted on. They ask which revision to try first.

options.label: Outline the cup with a thick dark line so it separates from the cloth, since a crisp edge makes the cup read as a separate solid object
Make the whole cup a uniform pale grey so it matches the cloth's lightness, since similar values will stop the two shapes competing
Judge values relatively: darken the cup's shadow side and lighten the cloth's darks, saving the lightest light for the highlight
Add dense hatching over the cloth so its texture draws the eye away from the cup, since a busy surface hides the harsh value jump

rubric: Reserving extremes and judging relative values lets the cup sit in space and in the same light.
Outlines, flat grey or hatching do not fix the value relationships.

items.prompt: You must plan a three-hour portrait that keeps a convincing likeness, soft light, and room to correct. Which sequence satisfies all three?

options.label: Block in measured shapes, establish value masses, then refine edges and add final accents
Render the eyes fully, then build outward feature by feature so likeness is secured early
Draw a detailed outline, then fill it with hatching to soften the light
Lay the full tonal range at once, then adjust the shapes using the eraser

rubric: Measured structure first, then value masses, then edges keeps changes cheap and preserves soft light.
Rendering early or outlining first locks in errors.

items.prompt: You must draw a corridor floor of identical square tiles receding to a vanishing point, using only construction lines. Which method fits?

options.label: Space the tiles by equal steps along the receding lines, matching the first tile's depth in the picture plane
Shrink each row's depth by a fixed tenth of the previous row's depth, repeating until the horizon is reached
Draw a diagonal across the first tile and extend it through the row crossings
Draw each far tile by eye, then adjust each row until the spacing looks even to the viewer

rubric: A diagonal construction gives foreshortened equal depths consistently.
Equal steps ignore foreshortening and the fixed ratio is arbitrary.

items.prompt: Design a value plan for a night scene lit by one candle. Constraints: the face is the focal point, shadows stay readable, and no flat black areas. Which plan fits?

options.label: Put the lightest lights and widest range on the face; keep surroundings in close dark mid-values
Give the whole sheet an even mid-grey tone so that no detail is lost in the shadows and the face stays visible
Spread bright accents evenly across the sheet so every object catches some candlelight and shadows stay readable
Make everything outside the face solid black to maximise contrast and push the face forward as the focal point

rubric: Concentrating the range at the focal point and keeping close dark values satisfies every constraint.
Even grey, solid black or spread-out accents remove the focus or the readability.

items.prompt: A figure drawing has correct proportions but a stiff, upright pose. Which rebuild keeps the proportions and adds rhythm?

options.label: Add loose hatching behind the figure and vary the marks' direction so the whole drawing looks more energetic
Set a line of action and counter-tilt shoulders against hips, then re-fit the measured masses
Redraw the figure smaller on the page and soften the contours so the pose feels more relaxed and natural
Thicken the outline on one side and lighten the other so that the figure appears to lean into the space

rubric: A line of action with opposed shoulder and hip tilts creates rhythm while measured masses preserve proportion.
Line weight, size or background marks do not change the pose.

items.prompt: Design a warm-up that trains accurate measuring and weakens the habit of drawing remembered symbols, such as an almond-shaped eye. Which exercise fits?

options.label: Fill a page with quick eye symbols until they look natural
Trace a reference photo so that the proportions are guaranteed to be right
Draw from memory the features you know best, then compare them with a photo
Copy a reference turned upside down, building it from negative shapes and angles

rubric: Inverting the reference and using negative shapes hinders naming and forces observation of actual relationships.
Memory drawing and repetition reinforce symbols, and tracing trains no measuring.

items.prompt: You plan a five-minute gesture drawing that must feel alive yet stay believable in weight and balance. Which elements belong in the plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: Start with one continuous line of action that follows the pose's main movement
Mark the weight-bearing leg and the balance line down from the neck
Measure the head and use it to lock the exact size of each feature
Outline the contour of the face in fine detail first to fix the likeness

rubric: A line of action and weight-balance marks capture the movement and stability quickly.
Early facial detail and exact measuring take too long for a five-minute gesture.

items.prompt: You sketch a street outdoors for 40 minutes. The sun moves, so the shadows keep shifting, but the drawing needs consistent form and light. Which plan meets all of these constraints?

options.label: Map the main shadow shapes early, treat them as fixed, and build the drawing within them
Draw in line only and leave all shadows out, so that changing light never conflicts with the drawing
Wait until the light settles, then begin drawing once the shadows have stopped moving
Update every shadow each time it moves, so that the drawing always matches the scene as it is now

rubric: Committing to one light state keeps form and light consistent despite the changing scene.
Continual updating produces contradictory light, and line-only or waiting does not meet the constraints.
